templates.name: Modifier placement: past participial opener (incl. Compared with that of)
Subject-verb agreement, relative pronoun or possessive inside subject
Finite vs nonfinite, finite main verb
Plural vs possessive nouns: one- or two-slot spelling grid
Finite vs nonfinite, to-infinitive (purpose or after “the first”)
Subject-verb agreement, quantifier or compound subject

items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (By + -ing), passage-final blank; the agent is the right subject
items.passage: Malleefowl, ground-dwelling birds native to Australia, incubate their eggs in an enormous mound of sand and decomposing vegetation. By scraping away or adding material as temperatures fluctuate, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the mound stays near 33°C, and the male checks its temperature by probing the sand with his beak.
the male keeps the mound near 33°C, checking its temperature by probing the sand with his beak.
the male’s constant labor keeps the mound near 33°C, a temperature he checks by probing the sand with his beak.
it is the male who keeps the mound near 33°C, checking its temperature with his beak.
items.explanation: The opening phrase describes someone scraping away or adding material to the mound, which only the bird can do. Choice B places “the male” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the male bird does the scraping and adding.

A.why_wrong: “The mound” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the mound scrapes away and adds material.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “the male’s constant labor,” not the male, so the sentence says that the labor scrapes away and adds material.

D.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

items.notes: Subject: malleefowl mound incubation (science, behavior). No named researchers. Band 6: plain agent key as in 188f7e3c (3.18); three recipes W, P, E; options 16 to 19 words, key not the longest; the male is not named in the passage, so the key does not echo it.

band7.why: Plain agent key (the male) with W, P and E distractors, the band-6 shape of 188f7e3c (3.18); band_target 6 as planned.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: past participial opener (Written in), mid-sentence blank; right subject is the person’s memoir, not the person
items.passage: After her husband died in 1689, Glikl of Hameln, a Jewish businesswoman in Hamburg, began composing an account of her life for her children. Written in Yiddish over nearly thirty years, ______ business negotiations, family disputes, and epidemics with remarkable candor.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Glikl, who addressed the work to her children, describes
Glikl’s children received from their mother a record of
there are descriptions, addressed to Glikl’s children, of
Glikl’s memoir, addressed to her children, describes
items.explanation: Something written in Yiddish over nearly thirty years must be a piece of writing, not a person. Choice D places “Glikl’s memoir” right after the phrase, so the phrase correctly describes the memoir.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the author keeps every fact
A.why_wrong: “Glikl” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that Glikl herself was written in Yiddish.

B.recipe: agent in possessive (P), wrong head noun
B.why_wrong: The head of “Glikl’s children” is “children,” so the sentence says that her children were written in Yiddish.

C.why_wrong: The word “there” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a noun it can describe.

items.notes: Subject: Glikl of Hameln’s Yiddish memoir (literature, history). Band 6: the key is a possessive noun phrase whose head (memoir) is what the opener describes, and two options start with “Glikl’s,” so the possessive form does not point to the key. The passage says “an account of her life”; the key paraphrases it as “memoir.”

band7.why: Possessive key whose head (memoir) is what the opener describes, with the obvious noun Glikl in A and a second “Glikl’s” option in B so form does not point to the key; band_target 6 as planned, reads strong 6.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener (Lying), passage-final blank; right subject is a property built on the obvious noun (the positions recorded in the logbooks)
items.passage: Nineteenth-century commercial whalers off Alaska logged the locations where they encountered sea ice. Lying far south of the ice edge documented by satellites each summer—in some years by hundreds of kilometers—______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the ice-edge positions in the whalers’ logbooks reveal how far the summer ice has since retreated.
the whalers’ logbooks contain ice-edge positions revealing how far the summer ice has since retreated.
it is clear from the whalers’ logbooks how far the summer ice has since retreated.
the summer ice’s retreat since then is revealed by the ice-edge positions in the whalers’ logbooks.
items.explanation: The opening phrase, interrupted by the aside between the dashes, describes something located far south of today’s summer ice edge: the positions of the ice edge that the whalers recorded. Choice A places “the ice-edge positions in the whalers’ logbooks” right after the phrase, so the phrase correctly describes those positions.

B.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the obvious noun, one level off, keeps every fact
B.why_wrong: “The whalers’ logbooks” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the logbooks themselves lie far south of the modern ice edge.

C.recipe: expletive opener (E), extraposed it on another noun
C.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving the phrase without a noun it can logically describe.

D.recipe: nominalised subject (N) borrowing the opener’s own noun
D.why_wrong: The subject is “the summer ice’s retreat,” so the sentence illogically says that the retreat lies far south of the modern ice edge.

items.notes: Subject: whaleship logbooks off Alaska as a record of past Arctic sea ice (science, climate). No named researchers or study. Band 7 on the property-key pattern of 2dd1b8bf and 8b017d4e (3.27) applied to the -ing opener of 2bca654a (3.21), with a dash aside inside the opener as in 2bca654a and fced396a (3.26) so the participle sits 19 words from the blank; the key’s head is the positions, built on the logbooks; options 14 to 19 words, key not the longest.
band7_moves: opener describes a location that only the recorded ice-edge positions can have, so the right subject is a noun phrase built on the obvious noun (property key, as 2dd1b8bf and 8b017d4e)
hardest distractor (B) starts with the obvious noun, the logbooks, and keeps every fact
a nominalised distractor (D) starts with the summer ice, the noun the opener itself names
dash aside inside the opener (as 2bca654a and fced396a) puts the participle Lying 19 words before the blank
key paraphrases the passage (“ice-edge positions” for “the locations where they encountered sea ice”)

band7.why: Property opener (where the logged positions lie) on the 2bca654a -ing frame with a dash aside as in fced396a, participle 19 words from the blank; the key is a noun phrase built on the obvious noun (positions in the logbooks) while B makes the logbooks themselves the subject and keeps every fact. After the fix no distractor mirrors the key.

fixes: option C was the key wrapped in an it-cleft (“it is the ice-edge positions ... that reveal”), a wrong option mirroring the key; rebuilt as an extraposed “it is clear from the whalers’ logbooks how far ...” (14 words), still dangling for the same reason, as 2bca654a builds its cleft on another noun (hardened through the tested rule)

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: plural head behind a singular possessor, with a long intervener whose relative clause has singular verbs
items.passage: In ninth-century Baghdad, three brothers known as the Banu Musa compiled the Book of Ingenious Devices. The book’s designs for roughly a hundred mechanisms, among them a lamp that automatically trims its wick and replenishes its oil, ______ among the earliest surviving descriptions of self-regulating machines.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the plural noun “designs” (“The book’s designs”), not “book,” “lamp,” or “oil.” The plural verb “rank” agrees with it; everything from “for roughly a hundred mechanisms” to “oil” only describes the designs.

A.recipe: wrong number, present (agrees with the possessor book’s or the nearest noun)
A.why_wrong: “Ranks” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural subject “designs.”

B.why_wrong: “Has ranked” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural subject “designs.”

D.why_wrong: “Is ranking” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural subject “designs.”

items.notes: Subject: the Banu Musa brothers’ Book of Ingenious Devices (history of technology). Band 7 on f10b7ce4 (3.25): plural head behind a singular possessor, here with 18 words between head and blank. Not the 3.23 frame (compound possessor + singular head + of-phrase).
band7_moves: plural head (designs) behind a singular possessor (book’s), right after a singular title, as f10b7ce4 (3.25)
intervener of 18 words with three singular nouns (lamp, wick, oil) and a relative clause whose own verbs (trims, replenishes) are singular
the noun right before the blank is singular, so the nearest-noun reading picks the wrong number
options: wrong number in three tenses, key the shortest

band7.why: Plural head (designs) behind a singular possessor (book’s) as f10b7ce4, 18 words to the blank with singular attractors (lamp, wick, oil) and a relative clause carrying its own singular verbs (trims, replenishes); all three distractors singular, as 863065c7.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: main verb after a long noun-clause subject (What ... have found ...) that contains its own finite verbs
items.passage: What linguists documenting Kata Kolok, a sign language that emerged in a single Balinese village, consider most distinctive about it ______ the way its signers indicate locations: they point in the actual direction of a place, even one far beyond the village.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence’s subject is the whole clause “What linguists ... consider most distinctive about it,” and that subject still needs a main verb. The finite verb “is” supplies it; the verbs inside the subject (“emerged,” “consider”) belong to the clauses within it.

B.recipe: nonfinite -ing where a finite verb is needed
B.why_wrong: The participle “being” doesn’t supply the sentence with a main verb, so the result is a fragment.

C.why_wrong: The infinitive “to be” doesn’t supply the sentence with a main verb, so the result is a fragment.

D.why_wrong: The participle “having been” doesn’t supply the sentence with a main verb, so the result is a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: Kata Kolok, the village sign language of Bengkala, Bali (social science, linguistics). No named researchers. R2_finite_main has no band-7 officials, so this is a strong band 6 (plan asked for 7). Differs from b1’s dash-interrupter frame: the subject is a what-clause containing an appositive and two finite verbs, 20 words before the blank.

band7.why: R2_finite_main has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7 (plan asked for 7); a strong band 6: what-clause subject holding an appositive and two finite verbs, 20 words before the blank.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: two-slot grid; plural noun decided by the verb inside the options, generic plural possessor with no determiner
items.passage: British artists the Singh Twins adapt Mughal miniature painting to contemporary subjects. Densely populated with figures and jokes, their ______ patience with details that emerge on repeated viewing.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Paintings” must be a plain plural: it is the subject of the plural verb “reward,” and nothing belongs to it. “Viewers’” must be a plural possessive: the patience belongs to viewers in general, and a singular possessive would need a word such as “a” before it (“a viewer’s patience”).

A.recipe: needless apostrophe on the plain plural
A.why_wrong: “Painting’s” is a singular possessive, which leaves the sentence without a subject for “reward” and without a verb.

B.recipe: wrong possessor number (singular possessive with no determiner)
B.why_wrong: “Viewer’s” is singular; the sentence describes viewers in general, and a singular count noun here would need a determiner such as “a.”

C.why_wrong: “Viewers” is a plain plural, but the patience belongs to the viewers, so a possessive is needed.

items.notes: Subject: the Singh Twins, British painters in the Indian miniature tradition (arts). Band 7 on 2784cbaf (3.24): the second slot is a generic plural possessor whose singular form fails only because it lacks a determiner. Each distractor is wrong in one slot; the key shares “paintings reward” with B and C and “viewers’” with A.
band7_moves: generic plural possessor with no determiner (viewers’ patience), the rule edge case of 2784cbaf (3.24)
two slots, with the first slot’s form fixed by the verb inside the options rather than by a nearby noun
each distractor wrong in exactly one slot, so no option is rejected on sight
the word right before the blank (their) gives no number cue for either slot

band7.why: Slot-for-slot copy of 2784cbaf (3.24): plain plural in slot 1, generic plural possessor in slot 2 whose singular form fails only for want of a determiner; each distractor wrong in one slot.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: purpose to-infinitive after a compound past-tense predicate; the -ing option would attach to the nearest noun
items.passage: In 2011, Dutch engineers dredged about 21 million cubic meters of sand from the floor of the North Sea and sculpted it into a hook-shaped artificial peninsula off the coast ______ whether wind, waves, and currents would gradually redistribute the sand along the coastline.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence already has its subject and verbs (“engineers dredged ... and sculpted”). The blank begins a phrase explaining why the engineers built the peninsula, and the infinitive “to learn” expresses that purpose.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed (second verb with no conjunction)
A.why_wrong: Without “and” before it, the finite verb “learned” can’t be added to the engineers’ actions.

C.why_wrong: Without a comma, “learning” attaches to the nearest noun, so the sentence illogically suggests that the coast or the peninsula is learning.

D.why_wrong: “Had learned” is a finite verb with no subject or conjunction, and it would place the learning before the dredging.

items.notes: Subject: the Sand Motor (Zandmotor), the 2011 sand peninsula off South Holland (science, coastal engineering). No named people. R2_to_inf has no band-7 officials, so this is a strong band 6 (plan asked for 7). Verb chosen so the -ing option cannot be read as a sensible reduced relative on “coast” or “peninsula” (a peninsula cannot learn); options are not 3.19’s “and V-ing” set.

band7.why: R2_to_inf has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7 (plan asked for 7); a strong band 6 on 512f0ac9 (3.19), the -ing distractor rejected for the same reason CB gives there.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head with a relative clause and an appositive full of plurals
items.passage: At the flower auction in Aalsmeer, the Netherlands, prices are displayed on an enormous clock whose hand starts high and sweeps downward. The buyer who stops the hand, one of hundreds of competing wholesalers and exporters, ______ the flowers at the indicated price.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “buyer.” The singular verb “buys” agrees with it; the plural nouns “hundreds,” “wholesalers,” and “exporters” only describe the buyer.

A.why_wrong: “Buy” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “buyer.”

B.why_wrong: “Are buying” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “buyer.”

D.why_wrong: “Have bought” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “buyer.”

items.notes: Subject: the Aalsmeer flower auction’s descending clock (social science, economics). Medium: one appositive of plurals between head and blank; the noun right before the blank is plural, so it does not cue the key.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: subject pronoun (with verb) a sentence after a plural antecedent, singular nouns between
items.passage: Noctilucent clouds, which form roughly 80 kilometers above the planet’s surface, are typically visible only during summer at high latitudes. Well after sunset, when an observer on the ground is surrounded by darkness, ______ illuminated by sunlight, glowing an eerie electric blue against the darkening sky.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The pronoun refers back to “noctilucent clouds,” a plural noun, so the plural pronoun “they” is needed. The singular nouns “an observer,” “the ground,” and “darkness” can’t be what remains illuminated and glows blue.

A.why_wrong: The singular pronoun “it” doesn’t agree with the plural antecedent “noctilucent clouds.”

B.why_wrong: The singular pronoun “one” doesn’t agree with the plural antecedent “noctilucent clouds.”

C.why_wrong: The singular pronoun “this” doesn’t agree with the plural antecedent “noctilucent clouds” and has no clear referent.

items.notes: Subject: noctilucent clouds (science, atmosphere). Medium on 2.4: pronoun + verb options so the verb gives no number cue; the antecedent is a sentence back, with singular nouns between it and the blank, the nearest of them (darkness) singular.

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: singular possessor + plural noun across a three-word phrase
items.passage: Abdulla Qodiriy’s Bygone Days, serialized in the early 1920s, is widely considered the first modern Uzbek novel. Set in the 1840s, it chronicles a young Tashkent merchant’s doomed marriage to a woman from Margilan, and many of the ______ unfold in the streets and bazaars of Tashkent, the author’s birthplace.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The scenes belong to one novel, Bygone Days, so the singular possessive “novel’s” is needed. Nothing belongs to the scenes, and the passage refers to many of them, so “scenes” is a plain plural.

B.recipe: missing apostrophe on the possessor + needless apostrophe on the plural
B.why_wrong: “Novels” is a plain plural rather than a possessive, and “scene’s” is a singular possessive where a plain plural is needed.

C.why_wrong: “Novels’” is a plural possessive, but the scenes belong to a single novel.

D.recipe: needless apostrophe on the plain plural
D.why_wrong: “Scene’s” is a singular possessive, but nothing belongs to the scenes and there are many of them.

items.notes: Subject: Abdulla Qodiriy’s Bygone Days (O‘tkan kunlar), the first Uzbek novel (literature). Partial grid as in 2.24; the passage also uses “merchant’s” and “author’s,” so apostrophes elsewhere do not point to the key.

fixes: “the doomed marriage of a Tashkent merchant’s son” made “a young Tashkent merchant’s doomed marriage to a woman from Margilan”: the hero is himself a young merchant (his father a Tashkent notable) and his bride is from Margilan; the possessive decoy in the passage is kept; word_count 47 to 50

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: “Each of the [plural]” subject, be-family options
items.passage: During Japan’s Edo period (1603–1868), people from samurai to farmers hung wooden tablets called sangaku in temples and shrines. Each of the roughly 900 surviving tablets ______ inscribed with at least one mathematical problem, typically accompanied by a diagram.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is “each,” which is singular, so the singular verb “is” is needed. The plural noun “tablets” comes inside the phrase “of the roughly 900 surviving tablets” and doesn’t change the subject’s number.

A.why_wrong: “Are” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “each.”

C.why_wrong: “Were” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “each.”

D.why_wrong: “Have been” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “each.”

items.notes: Subject: sangaku, Edo-period temple geometry tablets (history, mathematics). Medium on 2.23 (“Every last second of ...”): quantifier head with a plural noun right before the blank.

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener describing a person, mid-sentence blank
items.passage: A court painter to the Mughal emperor Jahangir, who collected rare animals, ______ a zebra brought to the court in 1621, recording its stripes with near-scientific precision.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Ustad Mansur’s best-known works include a portrait of
it was Ustad Mansur who painted a portrait of
Ustad Mansur painted a portrait of
a portrait by Ustad Mansur depicts
items.explanation: The opening noun phrase, “A court painter to the Mughal emperor Jahangir,” describes a person. Choice C places “Ustad Mansur” right after it, so the phrase correctly describes the painter.

A.why_wrong: The subject is “Ustad Mansur’s best-known works,” so the sentence illogically calls his works a court painter.

B.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, leaving “a court painter” without a person to describe.

D.why_wrong: “A portrait” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the portrait was a court painter.

items.notes: Subject: Ustad Mansur’s zebra study for Jahangir (arts, Mughal painting). Medium on 2.10: short, clear opener; key is the plain name + verb.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: main verb after an appositive
items.passage: Sea lilies, flowerlike relatives of sea stars, ______ themselves to the seafloor with a long stalk topped by a crown of feathery arms that filter food from the water.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “sea lilies” needs a main verb, and the finite verb “attach” supplies it. The phrase between the commas only describes sea lilies.

A.why_wrong: The participle “attaching” doesn’t give the sentence a main verb.

B.why_wrong: The participle “having attached” doesn’t give the sentence a main verb.

C.why_wrong: The infinitive “to attach” doesn’t give the sentence a main verb.

items.notes: Subject: sea lilies, stalked crinoids (science, marine biology). Replaces frost flowers (a second sea-ice subject beside item 03). Canonical easy option set.

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: main verb right after a short subject
items.passage: Over 2,000 years ago, artisans in China began manufacturing Han purple, a synthetic pigment used to decorate pottery and painted figurines. The pigment ______ barium, copper, and silicon, which bond only when heated to nearly 1,000°C.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “the pigment” needs a main verb, and the finite verb “contains” supplies it.

A.why_wrong: The participle “containing” doesn’t give the sentence a main verb.

C.why_wrong: The infinitive “to contain” doesn’t give the sentence a main verb.

D.why_wrong: The participle “having contained” doesn’t give the sentence a main verb.

items.notes: Subject: Han purple pigment (science, chemistry). Two sentences, blank in the second, as 1.30.

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: subject pronoun for a named person
items.passage: In 1972, French filmmaker Sarah Maldoror released Sambizanga, a film about the early days of Angola’s war for independence from Portugal. Because Angola was still under Portuguese rule, ______ shot the film in neighboring Congo, casting many members of African liberation movements.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The person who shot the film is Sarah Maldoror, a single woman named in the first sentence, so the singular pronoun “she” is needed.

B.why_wrong: The plural pronoun “they” doesn’t agree with the singular antecedent “Sarah Maldoror.”

C.recipe: wrong kind (thing pronoun for a person)
C.why_wrong: “It” refers to a thing, not a person, and nothing in the sentence that “it” could refer to shot the film.

D.why_wrong: “One” doesn’t refer clearly to Sarah Maldoror, the filmmaker named in the first sentence.

items.notes: Subject: Sarah Maldoror’s Sambizanga, shot in Congo (arts, film).

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: unfamiliar plural head with an appositive
items.passage: Tafoni, rounded cavities that give some sandstone and granite outcrops a honeycomb pattern, ______ especially common on coastlines, where growing salt crystals loosen grains of rock.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Tafoni” is a plural noun, as the appositive “rounded cavities” shows, so the plural verb “are” is needed.

A.why_wrong: “Is” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural subject “tafoni.”

B.why_wrong: “Was” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural subject “tafoni.”

D.why_wrong: “Has been” is singular and doesn’t agree with the plural subject “tafoni.”

items.notes: Subject: tafoni, honeycomb weathering (science, geology). As 1.28 (“ayllus”), an unfamiliar plural; the appositive supplies the cue.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: named person + relative clause
items.passage: Edith Clarke, who in 1921 invented a calculator for solving equations about power lines, ______ the first woman to teach electrical engineering at an American university.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is “Edith Clarke,” a single person, so the singular verb “was” is needed. The relative clause between the commas only describes her.

A.why_wrong: “Were” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Edith Clarke.”

B.why_wrong: “Are” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Edith Clarke.”

C.why_wrong: “Have been” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “Edith Clarke.”

items.notes: Subject: Edith Clarke, electrical engineer (science, engineering history). As 1.4: name + clause, be-family options.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement: singular head + appositive name, lexical-verb options
items.passage: Venezuelan writer Teresa de la Parra’s novel Ifigenia (1924) is structured as a letter followed by a diary. Its narrator, María Eugenia, ______ her frustrations after returning from Paris to Caracas, where her family pressures her toward a loveless marriage.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject is the singular noun “narrator,” renamed by “María Eugenia,” so the singular verb “records” is needed.

B.why_wrong: “Record” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “narrator.”

C.why_wrong: “Are recording” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “narrator.”

D.why_wrong: “Have recorded” is plural and doesn’t agree with the singular subject “narrator.”

items.notes: Subject: Teresa de la Parra’s Ifigenia (literature).

items.subtype: Tense: present for a general process, cued by present verbs in the same and previous sentence
items.passage: When a strong wind blows along a lake, it pushes water toward the downwind shore, temporarily raising the water level there. Once the wind subsides, the water ______ back and forth across the basin for hours, an oscillation known as a seiche.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passage describes a general process in the present tense (“blows,” “pushes,” “subsides”). The present tense verb “sloshes” fits that description.

A.recipe: simple past where present is needed
A.why_wrong: The past tense “sloshed” doesn’t fit a general process described in the present tense.

B.recipe: past perfect where present is needed
B.why_wrong: The past perfect “had sloshed” describes an action completed before another past action, which doesn’t fit this present-tense description.

D.why_wrong: “Would have sloshed” describes something that might have happened in the past, not a general process.

items.notes: Subject: lake seiches (science, earth science). Replaces the glass knifefish (a textbook subject).

items.subtype: Tense: present in a general description, cued by parallel present verbs
items.passage: In cantu a tenore, a polyphonic singing tradition from Sardinia, four men stand in a tight circle. While the lead singer ______ the verses of a poem, the other three accompany him with nonsense syllables, two of them producing a deep, guttural sound.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The passage describes how this style of singing is always performed, using the present tense (“stand,” “accompany”). The present tense verb “sings” matches.

A.recipe: simple past where present is needed
A.why_wrong: The past tense “sang” doesn’t match the present tense description (“stand,” “accompany”).

C.why_wrong: The past perfect “had sung” doesn’t match the present tense description.

D.why_wrong: The future perfect “will have sung” doesn’t match the present tense description.

items.notes: Subject: cantu a tenore, Sardinian four-voice singing (arts, music).

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: singular possessor + plural noun
items.passage: The talipot palm, native to southern India and Sri Lanka, may grow for 30 to 80 years without flowering. Eventually it produces an enormous branching inflorescence, the largest of any plant, containing millions of tiny blossoms. Once the ______ ripen, the tree dies.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The fruits belong to one palm, so the singular possessive “palm’s” is needed. Nothing belongs to the fruits, and “ripen” shows there is more than one, so “fruits” is a plain plural.

A.recipe: missing apostrophe on the possessor + needless apostrophe on the plural
A.why_wrong: “Palms” is a plain plural rather than a possessive, and “fruit’s” is a singular possessive.

B.recipe: needless apostrophe on the plain plural
B.why_wrong: “Fruit’s” is a singular possessive, but nothing belongs to the fruits.

D.why_wrong: “Palms’” is a plural possessive, but the passage describes a single palm.

items.notes: Subject: the talipot palm, which flowers once and dies (science, botany).

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: purpose to-infinitive after a complete clause
items.passage: For centuries, Maya beekeepers on Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula have maintained colonies of a stingless bee called xunan kab in hollow logs ______ its honey, which is prized for its medicinal properties.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence already has its subject and verb (“beekeepers ... have maintained”). The infinitive “to harvest” begins a phrase that explains why the beekeepers maintain the colonies.

A.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed
A.why_wrong: The finite verb “harvested” can’t follow the complete clause without a conjunction.

B.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed
B.why_wrong: The finite verb “harvests” can’t follow the complete clause without a conjunction.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite is needed
C.why_wrong: The finite verb “is harvesting” can’t follow the complete clause without a conjunction.

items.notes: Subject: Maya stingless beekeeping (xunan kab, Melipona beecheii) in Yucatán (social science, anthropology).

items.subtype: Tense: past perfect for an earlier past (“before” a dated past event)
items.passage: In 1947, a priest in the Colombian village of Sutatenza began broadcasting reading and arithmetic lessons to farmworkers over a small radio transmitter. Many of the adults who gathered around radios to follow the lessons ______ a school before.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The adults gathered around radios in the past, beginning in 1947, and “before” points to a time earlier than that. The past perfect “had never attended” places their lack of schooling before the lessons began.

B.why_wrong: The present tense “never attend” doesn’t fit events of 1947 and earlier.

C.why_wrong: The future tense “will never attend” doesn’t fit events of 1947 and earlier.

D.why_wrong: The present progressive “are never attending” doesn’t fit events of 1947 and earlier.

items.notes: Subject: Radio Sutatenza, Colombian radio schools (social science, education and media). Simple past left out of the options so it cannot be defended with “before.”

items.subtype: Tense: simple past cued by a date
items.passage: Murals discovered at Afrasiyab, the archaeological site of ancient Samarkand in present-day Uzbekistan, depict ambassadors presenting gifts. In the 660s, when the murals were painted, the city ______ the capital of a Sogdian kingdom ruled by Varkhuman.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence describes the 660s, a time in the past, so the past tense verb “was” is needed.

A.why_wrong: The present tense “is” doesn’t fit an event in the 660s.

C.why_wrong: The future tense “will be” doesn’t fit an event in the 660s.

D.why_wrong: The present perfect “has been” doesn’t fit an event that ended long ago in the 660s.

items.notes: Subject: King Varkhuman and the Afrasiyab murals, Samarkand (history).
